stem: The value of \(1 + i^2 + i^4 + i^6 + \dots + i^{2n}\) is
solution: The sum is \(\sum_{k=0}^{n}(i^2)^k = \sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\). If \(n\) is even the sum is \(1\); if \(n\) is odd the sum is \(0\). So the value is always \(0\) or \(1\), i.e. never negative. Matches option D.

stem: If \(i^2=-1\), then the value of \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{200} i^n\) is
solution: Every four consecutive powers sum to zero: \(i+i^2+i^3+i^4=i-1-i+1=0\). Since \(200\) is a multiple of \(4\) (50 full blocks), the total is \(0\). Matches option C.

stem: If \(\left(\dfrac{1-i}{1+i}\right)^{100} = a+ib\), then :
If \((x+iy)(2-3i)=4+i\), then
solution: Expanding, \((2x+3y)+i(-3x+2y)=4+i\). So \(2x+3y=4\) and \(-3x+2y=1\). Solving gives \(x=\tfrac{5}{13}\) and \(y=\tfrac{14}{13}\). Matches option B.

stem: The square root of \(3+4i\) is
solution: Let \(\sqrt{3+4i}=a+bi\). Then \(a^2-b^2=3\) and \(2ab=4\); also \(a^2+b^2=|3+4i|=5\). Hence \(a^2=4,\ b^2=1\), and since \(ab>0\), \(a=2,\ b=1\). So \(\sqrt{3+4i}=\pm(2+i)\). Matches option C.

stem: If \((2+i\sqrt{3})\) is a root of the equation \(x^2+px+q=0\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are real, then \((p,q)\) equals to:
solution: For real coefficients the conjugate \(2-i\sqrt{3}\) is also a root. Sum of roots \(=4=-p\Rightarrow p=-4\); product \(=4+3=7=q\). So \((p,q)=(-4,7)\).
reviewNote: FLAWED: printed options A and C are identical, both \((-4,7)\). The correct pair \((-4,7)\) appears twice. Keyed A (first occurrence).

stem: The conjugate of \(\dfrac{1}{3+4i}\) is
solution: \(\dfrac{1}{3+4i}=\dfrac{3-4i}{25}\). Its conjugate is \(\dfrac{3+4i}{25}=\dfrac{1}{25}(3+4i)\). Matches option B.

stem: The conjugate of the complex number \(\dfrac{2+5i}{4-3i}\) is
solution: \(\dfrac{2+5i}{4-3i}=\dfrac{(2+5i)(4+3i)}{25}=\dfrac{8+6i+20i-15}{25}=\dfrac{-7+26i}{25}\). Its conjugate is \(\dfrac{-7-26i}{25}\). Matches option A.

stem: If the conjugate of \((x+iy)(1-2i)\) be \(1+i\), then
solution: If the conjugate of \((x+iy)(1-2i)\) is \(1+i\), then \((x+iy)(1-2i)=\overline{1+i}=1-i\), so \(x+iy=\dfrac{1-i}{1-2i}\). Matches option C. (This gives \(x=\tfrac{3}{5},\ y=\tfrac{1}{5}\), so options A and D are false.)

stem: If \(z=x+iy\) then the value of \(\dfrac{z-\bar{z}}{z+\bar{z}}\) is
solution: \(z-\bar{z}=2iy\) and \(z+\bar{z}=2x\), so \(\dfrac{z-\bar{z}}{z+\bar{z}}=\dfrac{2iy}{2x}=\dfrac{iy}{x}\). Matches option D.

stem: If \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) are any two complex numbers, then \(|z_1+z_2|^2 + |z_1-z_2|^2\) is equal to :
solution: By the parallelogram law, \(|z_1+z_2|^2+|z_1-z_2|^2 = 2|z_1|^2 + 2|z_2|^2\). Matches option B.

stem: \(\left|(1+i)\dfrac{(2+i)}{(3+i)}\right|\) is equal to
solution: \(\left|(1+i)\dfrac{(2+i)}{(3+i)}\right|=\dfrac{|1+i|\,|2+i|}{|3+i|}=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{10}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{10}}{\sqrt{10}}=1\). Matches option A.
\(|z|=\dfrac{|3+4i|\,|5-7i|}{|7+5i|\,|4-3i|}=\dfrac{5\cdot\sqrt{74}}{\sqrt{74}\cdot 5}=1\). Matches option C.

stem: If \(z_1, z_2 \in C\) are such that \(|z_1+z_2|^2 = |z_1|^2 + |z_2|^2\) then \(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\) is -
solution: Expanding, \(|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2+2\,\mathrm{Re}(z_1\bar{z_2})=|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2\), so \(\mathrm{Re}(z_1\bar{z_2})=0\). Then \(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}=\dfrac{z_1\bar{z_2}}{|z_2|^2}\) has zero real part, i.e. it is purely imaginary. Matches option C.

stem: If \(\dfrac{2z_1}{3z_2}\) is a purely imaginary number, then \(\left|\dfrac{z_1-z_2}{z_1+z_2}\right|\) is equal to :
solution: If \(\dfrac{2z_1}{3z_2}\) is purely imaginary then \(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}=it\) for real \(t\). Then \(\left|\dfrac{z_1-z_2}{z_1+z_2}\right|=\left|\dfrac{it-1}{it+1}\right|=\dfrac{\sqrt{t^2+1}}{\sqrt{t^2+1}}=1\). Matches option B.

stem: If the number \(\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}\) is purely imaginary, then
solution: Writing \(z=x+iy\), the real part of \(\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}\) is \(\dfrac{x^2+y^2-1}{(x+1)^2+y^2}\). For a purely imaginary value this must be zero, giving \(x^2+y^2=1\), i.e. \(|z|=1\). Matches option B.

stem: The solution of the equation \(|z| - z = 1 + 2i\) is
solution: Let \(z=x+iy\). Then \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}-x-iy=1+2i\). Comparing imaginary parts, \(-y=2\Rightarrow y=-2\). Comparing real parts, \(\sqrt{x^2+4}-x=1\Rightarrow x=\tfrac{3}{2}\). So \(z=\tfrac{3}{2}-2i\). Matches option C.

stem: The argument of the complex number \(-1+i\sqrt{3}\) is
solution: The point \(-1+i\sqrt{3}\) lies in the second quadrant with reference angle \(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{1}=60^\circ\). So the argument is \(180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ\). Matches option A.

stem: If \(\arg(z)=\theta\), then \(\arg(\bar{z})\) is equal to
solution: If \(z=re^{i\theta}\) then \(\bar{z}=re^{-i\theta}\), so \(\arg(\bar{z})=-\theta\). Matches option D.

stem: The argument of the complex number \(\dfrac{13-5i}{4-9i}\) is -
solution: \(\dfrac{13-5i}{4-9i}=\dfrac{(13-5i)(4+9i)}{16+81}=\dfrac{52+117i-20i+45}{97}=\dfrac{97+97i}{97}=1+i\). So the argument is \(\arg(1+i)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Matches option B.

stem: The amplitude of \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{5} + i\left(1-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right)\) is
solution: Using \(1-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{5}=2\sin^2\dfrac{\pi}{10}\) and \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{5}=2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{10}\), the amplitude is \(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2\sin^2(\pi/10)}{2\sin(\pi/10)\cos(\pi/10)}=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{10}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{10}\). Matches option C.

stem: The amplitude of \(\dfrac{a+ib}{a-ib}\) is -
solution: Let \(\phi=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{b}{a}\), so \(a+ib=re^{i\phi}\) and \(a-ib=re^{-i\phi}\). Then \(\dfrac{a+ib}{a-ib}=e^{2i\phi}\), whose amplitude is \(2\phi\). Since \(\tan 2\phi=\dfrac{2\tan\phi}{1-\tan^2\phi}=\dfrac{2ab}{a^2-b^2}\), the amplitude is \(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2ab}{a^2-b^2}\). Matches option C.

stem: If \(z=-3+2i\), then \(\dfrac{1}{z}\) is equal to
solution: \(\dfrac{1}{z}=\dfrac{\bar{z}}{|z|^2}=\dfrac{-3-2i}{9+4}=\dfrac{-(3+2i)}{13}=-\dfrac{1}{13}(3+2i)\). Matches option B.

stem: Let \(z\) be a complex number such that \(|z|=4\) and \(\arg(z)=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\), then \(z\) equals-
solution: \(z=4\left(\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{6}+i\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)=4\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+i\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=-2\sqrt{3}+2i\). Matches option A.

stem: The polar form of \((-1+i)\) is-
solution: \(|-1+i|=\sqrt{2}\) and the point lies in the second quadrant, so \(\arg=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\). Hence \(-1+i=\sqrt{2}\left(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{4}+i\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)\). Matches option C.

stem: \(-1+\sqrt{-3}=re^{i\theta}\), then \(\theta\) is equal to -
solution: \(-1+\sqrt{-3}=-1+i\sqrt{3}\), which lies in the second quadrant with reference angle \(60^\circ\). So \(\theta=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\). Matches option A.

stem: \(|z_1+z_2| = |z_1| + |z_2|\) is possible, if
solution: Equality in the triangle inequality \(|z_1+z_2|=|z_1|+|z_2|\) holds exactly when \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) point in the same direction, i.e. \(\arg(z_1)=\arg(z_2)\). Matches option C.

stem: The value of \(\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2^2}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2^2}\right)\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2^3}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2^3}\right)\dots\infty\) is :
solution: The product equals \(\exp\!\left(i\pi\left(\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{8}+\dots\right)\right)=\exp(i\pi\cdot 1)=e^{i\pi}=-1\). Matches option A.

stem: One of the cube roots of unity is :
solution: The non-real cube roots of unity are \(\omega=\dfrac{-1+i\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(\omega^2=\dfrac{-1-i\sqrt{3}}{2}\). Matches option C.

stem: If \(1, \omega, \omega^2\) are the three cube roots of unity, then \((3+\omega^2+\omega^4)^6\) is
solution: Since \(\omega^4=\omega\), \(3+\omega^2+\omega^4=3+\omega+\omega^2=3+(-1)=2\). So \((2)^6=64\). Matches option C.

stem: The three value of \((8)^{1/3}\) are -
solution: The cube roots of \(8\) are \(2\cdot 1,\ 2\omega,\ 2\omega^2\), where \(\omega\) is a cube root of unity. Matches option B.

stem: If \(\alpha\) is an imaginary cube root of unity, then for \(n \in N\), the value of \(\alpha^{3n+1}+\alpha^{3n+3}+\alpha^{3n+5}\).
solution: Since \(\alpha^3=1\), \(\alpha^{3n+1}+\alpha^{3n+3}+\alpha^{3n+5}=\alpha+\alpha^3+\alpha^5=\alpha+1+\alpha^2=(\alpha+\alpha^2)+1=-1+1=0\). Matches option B.

stem: If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are imaginary cube roots of unity, then the value of \(\alpha^4 + \beta^{28} + \dfrac{1}{\alpha\beta}\) is :
solution: Take \(\alpha=\omega,\ \beta=\omega^2\). Then \(\alpha^4=\omega^4=\omega\), \(\beta^{28}=\omega^{56}=\omega^2\), and \(\alpha\beta=\omega^3=1\) so \(\dfrac{1}{\alpha\beta}=1\). Sum \(=\omega+\omega^2+1=0\). Matches option C.

stem: If \(\omega\) is the cube root of unity, then \((3+5\omega+3\omega^2)^2 + (3+3\omega+5\omega^2)^2\) is equal to -
solution: Using \(1+\omega+\omega^2=0\): \(3+5\omega+3\omega^2=3(1+\omega+\omega^2)+2\omega=2\omega\) and \(3+3\omega+5\omega^2=2\omega^2\). So \((2\omega)^2+(2\omega^2)^2=4\omega^2+4\omega^4=4(\omega^2+\omega)=4(-1)=-4\). Matches option B.

stem: The \(n^{th}\) roots of unity are in :
solution: The \(n\)-th roots of unity are \(1, \alpha, \alpha^2, \dots, \alpha^{n-1}\) with \(\alpha=e^{2\pi i/n}\), successive terms having a constant ratio \(\alpha\). Hence they are in GP. Matches option B.

stem: If \(z=x+iy\), then area of the triangle whose vertices are points \(z, iz, z+iz\) is :
solution: The vectors from \(z\) to \(iz\) and from \(z\) to \(z+iz\) are \(z(i-1)\) and \(iz\). The area is \(\tfrac12\big|\mathrm{Im}\big(z(i-1)\cdot\overline{iz}\big)\big|=\tfrac12|z|^2\). Matches option A.

stem: In which quadrant of the complex plane, the point \(\dfrac{1+2i}{1-i}\) lies?
solution: \(\dfrac{1+2i}{1-i}=\dfrac{(1+2i)(1+i)}{2}=\dfrac{1+i+2i-2}{2}=\dfrac{-1+3i}{2}\). The real part is negative and the imaginary part is positive, so it lies in the second quadrant. Matches option C.

stem: Let \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) be two complex number such that \(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}+\dfrac{z_2}{z_1}=1\), then
optB: \(z_1, z_2\) and the origin form a right angled triangle
optC: \(z_1, z_2\) and the origin form an equilateral triangle
solution: Let \(t=\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\). Then \(t+\dfrac{1}{t}=1\Rightarrow t^2-t+1=0\Rightarrow t=\dfrac{1\pm i\sqrt{3}}{2}=e^{\pm i\pi/3}\). So \(|z_1|=|z_2|\) and the angle between them is \(60^\circ\); with the origin they form an equilateral triangle. Matches option C.

stem: The equation \(z\bar{z} + (2-3i)z + (2+3i)\bar{z} + 4 = 0\) represents a circle of radius.
solution: Comparing with \(z\bar{z}+a\bar{z}+\bar{a}z+b=0\), here \(a=2-3i\) and \(b=4\), giving radius \(\sqrt{|a|^2-b}=\sqrt{(4+9)-4}=\sqrt{9}=3\). Matches option B.

stem: If \(\left|\dfrac{z-i}{z+i}\right|=1\), then locus of \(z\) is
solution: \(\left|\dfrac{z-i}{z+i}\right|=1\Rightarrow |z-i|=|z+i|\), i.e. \(z\) is equidistant from \(i\) and \(-i\). This is the real axis (x-axis). Matches option A.

stem: A complex number \(z\) is such that \(\arg\left(\dfrac{z-2}{z+2}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\). The points representing this complex number will lie on :
solution: The locus where the angle subtended by the segment joining \(2\) and \(-2\) is a constant \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) is an arc of a circle. Matches option D.

stem: If \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) are two complex numbers, then \(|z_1-z_2|\)
solution: The reverse triangle inequality gives \(|z_1-z_2|\geq |z_1|-|z_2|\). Matches option A.
reviewNote: FLAWED (multiple-correct): both A \((|z_1-z_2|\geq |z_1|-|z_2|)\) and C \((|z_1-z_2|\leq |z_1|+|z_2|)\) are always true. Keyed A as the reverse-triangle-inequality result distinctive to the difference (Q44 already tests the \(\leq\) form for the sum).

stem: If \(z_1, z_2\) are any two complex numbers, then:
solution: The triangle inequality states \(|z_1+z_2|\leq |z_1|+|z_2|\), with equality only when they are in the same direction. Matches option C.

stem: If \(|z| \leq 1\) then the minimum and maximum value of \(|z-3|\) are -
solution: \(z\) lies in the closed unit disk. The distance \(|z-3|\) from the point \(3\) ranges from \(3-1=2\) (minimum) to \(3+1=4\) (maximum). So the values are \(2\) and \(4\). Matches option D.

stem: For any complex number \(z\), the minimum value of \(|z| + |z-1|\) is
solution: \(|z|+|z-1|\) is the sum of distances from \(z\) to \(0\) and to \(1\); by the triangle inequality it is at least \(|1-0|=1\), attained for any \(z\) on the segment \([0,1]\). Matches option B.
